configurePresets.name: release-tests
configurePresets.description: Release build with the C++ tests enabled. Shares build/release with the 'release' preset ON PURPOSE: the release workflow packages out of build/release, so both presets must produce the executable at the same path. Re-running one preset over the other's tree only flips CODEHARBOR_BUILD_TESTS and reconfigures; it never leaves a stale binary behind.

configurePresets.name: mobile-desktop
configurePresets.displayName: Mobile shell on the workstation (Debug, both clients)
configurePresets.description: Builds the desktop client AND the mobile client (src/vt, src/mobile, codeharbor_mobile) for this workstation. This is how the mobile shell is developed and validated: it is plain Qt Quick with no device-only API, so it runs on a Linux/macOS/Windows desktop, and its tst_* targets run headless in the ordinary ctest suite. An NDK or an iPhone is needed to SHIP the mobile client, never to compile or test it.

configurePresets.name: mobile-base
configurePresets.description: Shared cross-compile settings for the Android and iOS clients. Qt ships no WebEngine for either platform, so the desktop client is off; the mobile presets do not build the web bundles either, because src/qml is never added. Tests are off because every tst_* target is a host executable that ctest would have to run, and a cross-compiled one cannot run here. Each platform preset names the Qt-for-<platform> prefix and CH_LIBSSH_PREFIX, the per-ABI libssh built from the in-tree vcpkg overlay (packaging/vcpkg-ports); how they are named differs per platform, because Android reaches Qt through Qt's own toolchain file and iOS through CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH - see each preset's own description. An unset CH_LIBSSH_PREFIX degrades to the documented CH_HAVE_LIBSSH=0 warning rather than a configure error.

configurePresets.name: android-base
configurePresets.description: Shared Android cross-compile settings. The toolchain is Qt's qt.toolchain.cmake, NOT the NDK's android.toolchain.cmake directly, and that choice is load-bearing rather than stylistic: the NDK toolchain sets CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH to the device sysroot and CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PACKAGE to ONLY, so find_package() cannot see anything outside that sysroot no matter what CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH says - Qt itself included. A configure with the NDK toolchain therefore fails at find_package(Qt6) with 'Could not find a package configuration file provided by Qt6' while Qt is installed and CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH names it. Qt's toolchain chainloads the NDK one and then prepends the Qt prefix to CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH, which is what makes the search work; it also sets ANDROID_STL to c++_shared, which is what Qt for Android is built against and what androiddeployqt bundles (libc++_shared.so), so the NDK's c++_static default cannot put two C++ runtimes in one process. Non-Qt packages outside the sysroot need the same treatment, which is why the per-ABI libssh is named TWICE, deliberately. QT_ADDITIONAL_PACKAGES_PREFIX_PATH is what puts the prefix on CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH, without which the sysroot restriction hides it - but Qt's toolchain appends /lib/cmake to each such entry when it also puts it on CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, and vcpkg installs this libssh's package configuration under <prefix>/share/libssh, so that spelling alone would not resolve. CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH therefore carries the plain prefix as well, which is the entry find_package(ssh CONFIG) resolves through. Both workflows assert the resulting 'libssh: found via' configure line rather than assuming it, because a libssh that is merely not found is only a warning and would ship a client that cannot connect to anything. An unset CH_LIBSSH_PREFIX degrades to the documented CH_HAVE_LIBSSH=0 warning rather than a configure error. ANDROID_SDK_ROOT must exist as a CMAKE variable and not only in the environment, because Qt's deployment-settings generation globs <sdk>/build-tools/* out of that variable at CONFIGURE time and aborts with 'Could not locate Android SDK build tools' when it is empty.

configurePresets.name: android-arm64
configurePresets.description: Release APK/AAB for 64-bit ARM devices. Needs ANDROID_NDK_ROOT, ANDROID_SDK_ROOT, QT_HOST_PATH (the host Qt, for moc/rcc/qmlcachegen) and QT_ANDROID_PATH (the Qt-for-Android prefix, e.g. .../6.10.0/android_arm64_v8a). API 28 is Qt 6.10's floor.

configurePresets.name: android-arm64-debug
configurePresets.description: Same toolchain as android-arm64 but a Debug build, in its own binary directory so a debuggable APK and a release APK can coexist.

configurePresets.name: ios-base
configurePresets.description: Shared iOS cross-compile settings. The toolchain is Qt's qt.toolchain.cmake for the same reason the Android preset uses it: CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=iOS puts CMake into cross-compile mode, where it points find_package at the SDK sysroot only, so Qt sitting outside that sysroot is not found and the configure dies at find_package(Qt6) with Qt installed and named on CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH. Qt's toolchain prepends its own prefix to CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH; the per-ABI libssh is named both as QT_ADDITIONAL_PACKAGES_PREFIX_PATH (which reaches CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH) and on CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH (the plain prefix, which is what find_package(ssh CONFIG) resolves through, because vcpkg installs the package configuration under <prefix>/share/libssh while Qt appends /lib/cmake to the former). Deployment target 17.0 is Qt 6.10's supported floor. Each concrete preset picks its own sysroot, and the simulator one additionally turns code signing off - a simulator runs the binary on the host CPU and checks no signature, which is what lets it build with no Apple credentials at all.

configurePresets.name: ios-arm64
configurePresets.description: Device build. Signing is deliberately left to the machine that runs it: set the development team through Xcode or -DCMAKE_XCODE_ATTRIBUTE_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=<id>, so no team identifier is baked into the repository.

configurePresets.name: ios-simulator
configurePresets.description: Simulator build for Apple Silicon hosts. Code signing is turned off outright: the simulator does not check it, and requiring it would make an unsigned CI machine unable to compile the client at all.
